最终答案原文: No—not as a causal conclusion, and not for both outcomes. In the NOAA incident data (6,649 complete cases), I compared fires classified as Full Suppression at the 75% threshold (5,627 cases in the model) with Other, using regressions of log(1 + outcome) that controlled for relative humidity, wind, ERC, precipitation, start year, region, cause, and start day of year, with HC3 robust confidence intervals. Full Suppression was associated with about 60% lower duration on the transformed scale (95% CI: 57%–63% lower; p<0.001). But the summed count of primary residences, commercial buildings, and outbuildings threatened was about 207% higher on the transformed scale (95% CI: 149%–278% higher; p<0.001). This does not show fewer buildings affected: the NOAA fields measure buildings threatened, not buildings actually damaged or destroyed. The result is observational, not evidence that suppression caused fires to end sooner or caused the difference in exposure; treatment selection, initial fire size/severity, and other unmeasured factors could explain the associations. Thus: a strong weather-adjusted association with shorter duration, but no support for fewer buildings threatened, and no causal determination.
标准答案原文: More aggressive suppression does not help fires end faster but helps fires affect less buildings.
